steps.hint: The 10 N was twice as far out, so the closer push must be twice as big.

steps.say: You just made 10 × 2 = 20 × 1: force times distance, matched on both sides. That product, force × distance, is the moment, the turning effect. Every balance question is moment = moment, and every moment is \(M = F \times d\).

steps: Identify the pivot and which forces turn clockwise vs anticlockwise
If given a mass, find its weight first with W = mg
For a balanced beam or lever: set clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
For gears: gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth
method_card.title: Moments, Levers and Gears
method_card.content:
A moment is the turning effect of a force: \(M = F \times d\), in newton metres (Nm).

The distance is measured perpendicular to the force, from the pivot, and must be in metres.

For a balanced beam or lever, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. If several forces act on one side, work out each moment and add them. Given a mass, find its weight first with \(W = mg\).

For gears, the gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth. A larger driven gear turns slower but with more force.

steps: Add up several moments on one side before balancing, or bring in the beam's own weight acting at its centre.
Gears change a torque: gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth. More teeth means more force (multiply) but slower turning (divide for speed).
Two ideas often chain: a lever makes a torque, then a gear scales it. Do them in order.
gold.title: Gold: chain the steps

example.question: A 10 N force acts 0.5 m from a lever pivot, driving a 10-tooth gear into a 30-tooth gear. Find the output torque.

steps: A moment is the turning effect of a force: \(M = F \times d\), measured in newton metres (Nm).
The distance d is measured perpendicular to the force, from the pivot, and must be in metres. Convert cm to m first (divide by 100).
Rearrange when the unknown is not the moment: \(F = M \div d\) or \(d = M \div F\).
bronze.title: Bronze: one moment, straight in

example.question: A force of 60 N acts 0.4 m from a pivot. Find the moment.

steps: If a value is given as a mass, turn it into weight before using it: \(W = mg\), with g = 9.8 N/kg.
For a balanced beam or lever, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. Set \(F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2\) and rearrange for the unknown.
For a resultant, work out each moment separately, then subtract the smaller from the larger.

gold.hint: Add both left moments, then balance against F × 0.7.

N</text><text x="106" y="52" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">1.5 m</text><text x="131" y="40" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">0.5 m</text><text x="153" y="52" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">0.7 m</text></svg>A beam is balanced on a pivot. On the left side: a 100 N force acts 0.5 m from the pivot, and a 200 N force acts 1.5 m from the pivot. What single force on the right, at 0.7 m from the pivot, is needed to balance the beam?

guided_steps.say: Two forces on the left, so add their moments, then balance the right.
The right force at 0.7 m must match: F × 0.7 = 350, so F = 350 ÷ 0.7. Clear the decimal by ×10: 3500 ÷ 7.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the total left moment.

misconceptions.message: 350 Nm is the total left moment: (100 × 0.5) + (200 × 1.5). Divide by 0.7 m to get the balancing force: 500 N.
With two forces on one side, work out each moment and add them: 50 + 300 = 350 Nm. Using only one force loses part of the turning effect.

gold.hint: Gear ratio = 60 ÷ 20; divide the speed by it.
gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver gear rotates at 120 rpm. Calculate the speed of the driven gear in rpm.

guided_steps.say: Gears change speed by the gear ratio. Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth.
A bigger driven gear turns slower, so divide the input speed by the ratio.

guided_steps.done: Back to 120 rpm, so 40 rpm is right.
guided_steps.hint: This should return the driver's speed.

misconceptions.message: A larger driven gear turns slower, so divide: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 rpm. Multiplying (120 × 3 = 360) speeds it up instead.
Gear ratio = driven ÷ driver = 60 ÷ 20 = 3, then divide the input speed by the ratio.

gold.hint: Gear ratio = 60 ÷ 20; multiply the force by it.
gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. If the input force is 15 N, calculate the output force (assuming no energy losses).

guided_steps.say: Gears also change force by the gear ratio. Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth.
A bigger driven gear gives more force, so multiply the input force by the ratio.

guided_steps.done: Back to 15 N, so 45 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: This should return the input force.

misconceptions.message: A larger driven gear gives more force, so multiply: 15 × 3 = 45 N. Dividing (15 ÷ 3 = 5) shrinks the force instead.
Gear ratio = driven ÷ driver = 60 ÷ 20 = 3, then multiply the input force by the ratio.

gold.hint: Include the beam's own weight at its centre, then balance.

N</text><text x="56" y="46" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">0.8 m</text><text x="146" y="46" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">1.2 m</text></svg>A uniform beam is 2.0 m long with mass 10 kg. The pivot is 0.8 m from the left end. A 50 N load hangs from the left end. Calculate the force needed at the right end to balance the beam. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Three forces act: the 50 N load (left of the pivot), the beam's own weight at its centre, and the unknown F (right of the pivot). Start with the beam's weight.
The weight acts at the centre, 1.0 m from the left end. The pivot is at 0.8 m, so the weight is 1.0 − 0.8 = 0.2 m to the right of the pivot.

guided_steps.pre: Anticlockwise moment (the 50 N load, 0.8 m left): 50 × 0.8 =
Clockwise moment from the beam weight: 98 × 0.2 =
guided_steps.hint: Weight × its distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.say: Balance: anticlockwise = clockwise, so 40 = 19.6 + F × 1.2. Take the beam's part across first.

guided_steps.hint: This is the moment F must provide.

guided_steps.done: Equals 40 Nm, so 17 N balances the beam.
guided_steps.hint: This should equal the anticlockwise moment.

misconceptions.message: The beam's own weight (10 × 9.8 = 98 N) makes a clockwise moment of 98 × 0.2 = 19.6 Nm. Leaving it out gives 50 × 0.8 = F × 1.2, so F = 33.3 N instead of 17 N.
A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre, 1.0 m from the left end, which is 0.2 m from the pivot.

gold.hint: Lever torque first, then multiply by the gear ratio.
gold.display: A lever is connected to an input gear with 15 teeth. A force of 12 N is applied 0.3 m from the pivot on the lever. The output gear has 45 teeth. Calculate the output torque (moment) from the gear system in Nm.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: the lever makes a torque, then the gears multiply it.
More teeth on the output gear means more torque, so multiply.

guided_steps.done: Back to 3.6 Nm, so 10.8 Nm is right.
guided_steps.hint: This should return the input torque.

misconceptions.message: 3.6 Nm is only the lever's input torque (12 × 0.3). The gears multiply it by the ratio 3: output torque = 3.6 × 3 = 10.8 Nm.
More teeth on the output gear means more torque, so multiply: 3.6 × 3 = 10.8 Nm. Dividing (3.6 ÷ 3 = 1.2) is the wrong way.

gold.hint: Balance effort and load moments, then divide by 0.05.
gold.display: A crowbar is used to lift a heavy stone. The effort of 80 N is applied 0.75 m from the pivot. The stone rests 0.05 m from the pivot. Calculate the maximum force exerted on the stone.

guided_steps.say: A crowbar is a lever: effort moment = load moment. Effort moment first.
The stone is only 0.05 m from the pivot. F × 0.05 = 60, so F = 60 ÷ 0.05. Dividing by 0.05 is the same as ×20.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the effort moment.

misconceptions.message: 60 Nm is the effort's moment (80 × 0.75). Divide by the load distance 0.05 m to get the force on the stone: 1200 N.
The load is much closer to the pivot, so the force is multiplied. Mechanical advantage = 0.75 ÷ 0.05 = 15, and 80 × 15 = 1200 N.

bronze.hint: Moment is force times distance; multiply 50 by 0.3.
bronze.display: A force of 50 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.

guided_steps.say: The moment is the turning effect: \(M = F \times d\). Here F = 50 N and d = 0.3 m, both ready to use.

guided_steps.pre: Multiply the digits first, ignoring the decimal: 50 × 3 =
Now put the decimal back. 0.3 is 3 tenths, so 150 ÷ 10 =
guided_steps.hint: One decimal place means divide by 10.

guided_steps.done: Back to 50 N, so 15 Nm is right.
guided_steps.hint: Moment ÷ distance should return the force.

misconceptions.message: Moment is force × distance, so 50 × 0.3 = 15 Nm. Dividing (50 ÷ 0.3 = 166.7) is the usual slip.

bronze.display: A moment of 20 Nm is produced by a force acting 0.4 m from a pivot. Calculate the force.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(M = F \times d\) to \(F = M \div d = 20 \div 0.4\).

guided_steps.pre: Dividing by 0.4 is awkward, so multiply both by 10. The moment 20 becomes 20 × 10 =

guided_steps.done: Back to 20 Nm, so 50 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Force × distance should give the moment.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to F = M ÷ d = 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 N. Multiplying (20 × 0.4 = 8) divides the wrong way round.

bronze.display: A force of 30 N creates a moment of 12 Nm. Calculate the perpendicular distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange to \(d = M \div F = 12 \div 30\).

guided_steps.pre: 12 ÷ 30 is less than 1. Simplify the fraction 12/30: top, 12 ÷ 6 =

guided_steps.hint: Divide the bottom by 6, so the fraction is 2/5.

guided_steps.done: Back to 12 Nm, so 0.4 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: Force × distance should give the moment.

misconceptions.message: Distance = M ÷ F = 12 ÷ 30 = 0.4 m. Dividing the other way (30 ÷ 12 = 2.5) inverts the equation.

bronze.hint: Multiply the force by the distance.
bronze.display: A spanner applies a force of 200 N at a distance of 1.5 m from the bolt. Calculate the moment about the bolt.

guided_steps.say: \(M = F \times d\). Force 200 N, distance 1.5 m.

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 N, so 300 Nm is right.
guided_steps.hint: Moment ÷ distance should give the force.

misconceptions.message: Moment = 200 × 1.5 = 300 Nm. Dividing (200 ÷ 1.5 = 133.3) is the wrong operation.

bronze.display: A moment of 36 Nm acts on a door handle. The handle is 0.6 m from the hinge. Calculate the force applied.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange to \(F = M \div d = 36 \div 0.6\).

guided_steps.pre: Multiply both by 10 to clear the decimal: 36 becomes

guided_steps.done: Back to 36 Nm, so 60 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Force × distance should give the moment.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange to F = M ÷ d = 36 ÷ 0.6 = 60 N. Multiplying (36 × 0.6 = 21.6) is the slip.

bronze.display: A force of 80 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.25 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.

guided_steps.say: \(M = F \times d\). Force 80 N, distance 0.25 m.

guided_steps.pre: 0.25 has two decimal places, so divide by 100: 2000 ÷ 100 =

guided_steps.done: Back to 80 N, so 20 Nm is right.
guided_steps.hint: Dividing by a quarter is the same as ×4.

misconceptions.message: Moment = 80 × 0.25 = 20 Nm. Dividing (80 ÷ 0.25 = 320) is the wrong way round.

bronze.display: A force of 15 N creates a moment of 45 Nm. Calculate the perpendicular distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange to \(d = M \div F = 45 \div 15\). Build up in fifteens.

guided_steps.pre: That leaves exactly one more 15, so 45 ÷ 15 =

misconceptions.message: Distance = M ÷ F = 45 ÷ 15 = 3 m. Dividing the other way (15 ÷ 45 = 0.33) inverts it.

bronze.hint: Balance the moments: 400 × 2.0 = F × 1.6, then divide.
bronze.display: A seesaw is balanced. A 400 N force acts 2.0 m from the pivot on the left. A force acts 1.6 m from the pivot on the right. What is the force on the right?

guided_steps.say: Balanced beam: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. Find the left moment first.
The right side must match: F × 1.6 = 800, so F = 800 ÷ 1.6. Clear the decimal by ×10: 8000 ÷ 16.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the left moment.

misconceptions.message: Balance the moments: 400 × 2.0 = F × 1.6, so F = 800 ÷ 1.6 = 500 N. Swapping the distances (400 × 1.6 ÷ 2.0 = 320) mixes up which arm is which.

silver.hint: Turn masses into weights, then balance the moments.
silver.display: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 122" role="img" aria-label="A seesaw on a central pivot: a 30 kilogram child 2 metres left of the pivot and a 60 kilogram adult an unknown distance to the right"><line x1="30" y1="64" x2="230" y2="64" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="130,64 119,92 141,92" fill="#60a5fa" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="currentColor"/><line x1="70" y1="64" x2="70" y2="90" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="70,96 65,87 75,87" fill="currentColor"/><line x1="178" y1="64" x2="178" y2="90" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="178,96 173,87 183,87" fill="currentColor"/><text x="70" y="112" font-family="Inter" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">30 kg</text><text x="178" y="112" font-family="Inter" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">60 kg</text><text x="100" y="56" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">2.0 m</text><text x="154" y="56" font-family="Inter" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">? m</text></svg>A child of mass 30 kg sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult of mass 60 kg sits on the other side. How far from the pivot must the adult sit to balance? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Turn the masses into weights with \(W = mg\), g = 9.8 N/kg.
Balance: child's moment = adult's moment. Child's moment = 294 × 2.0.
So 588 = 588 × d. Rearrange: d = 588 ÷ 588.

guided_steps.done: Equals 588 Nm, so 1.0 m balances it.
guided_steps.hint: This should equal the child's moment.

misconceptions.message: Each side is weight × its own distance: 294 × 2.0 = 588 × d, so d = 1.0 m. Pairing the adult's weight with the child's distance instead gives d = 4.0 m, which unbalances the seesaw.
Here mass and weight give the same distance because g cancels on both sides, but always turn mass into weight (W = mg) in the moment equation as a habit.

silver.display: A 600 N force acts 0.8 m from a pivot (clockwise). What force at 1.2 m from the pivot (anticlockwise) is needed to balance it?

guided_steps.say: Balanced beam: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. Left moment first.
Match on the right: F × 1.2 = 480, so F = 480 ÷ 1.2. Clear the decimal by ×10: 4800 ÷ 12.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the clockwise moment.

misconceptions.message: 480 Nm is the clockwise moment (600 × 0.8). You still divide by 1.2 m to get the balancing force: 480 ÷ 1.2 = 400 N.
Balance: 600 × 0.8 = F × 1.2, so F = 480 ÷ 1.2 = 400 N. Swapping the distances (600 × 1.2 ÷ 0.8 = 900) uses the wrong arm.

silver.hint: Find the load's weight first, then balance the moments.
silver.display: A nutcracker has the nut 0.08 m from the pivot and the handle 0.4 m from the pivot. A 5 kg mass is placed in the nutcracker. Calculate the force you need to apply at the handle to crack it. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: First the load's weight: \(W = mg = 5 \times 9.8\).
That weight sits 0.08 m from the pivot, so its moment = 49 × 0.08.
Your effort at 0.4 m must match: F × 0.4 = 3.92, so F = 3.92 ÷ 0.4.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the load's moment.

misconceptions.message: Use weight, not mass: W = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N. Then 49 × 0.08 = F × 0.4 gives F = 9.8 N. Using the mass 5 kg instead gives F = 1.0 N, ten times too small.

silver.hint: Work out both moments and subtract the smaller from the larger.
silver.display: A beam has a pivot in the centre. A 200 N force acts 1.0 m to the left of the pivot. A 150 N force acts 2.0 m to the right. Calculate the resultant moment. State the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). Give your answer as the magnitude only.

guided_steps.say: Work out each moment, then find the difference. \(M = F \times d\).
They turn opposite ways, so the resultant is the difference, in the direction of the larger.

guided_steps.pre: Sanity check: the larger moment minus the resultant should equal the opposing moment. 300 − 100 =
guided_steps.done: Equals 200 Nm, so 100 Nm is the leftover turning effect.
guided_steps.hint: This should match the anticlockwise moment.

misconceptions.message: The moments oppose, so subtract: 300 − 200 = 100 Nm clockwise. Adding them (200 + 300 = 500) ignores that they turn opposite ways.

silver.hint: Find the weight (mg) first, then multiply by the distance.
silver.display: An 8 kg mass hangs from a horizontal bar at a distance of 0.25 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment about the pivot. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Turn the mass into weight: \(W = mg = 8 \times 9.8\).
Now the moment of that weight at 0.25 m: M = 78.4 × 0.25.

guided_steps.done: Back to the weight, so 19.6 Nm is right.
guided_steps.hint: Dividing by a quarter is the same as ×4.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: W = 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 N, then M = 78.4 × 0.25 = 19.6 Nm. Using the mass 8 kg gives 8 × 0.25 = 2.0 Nm, which leaves out gravity.

silver.hint: Balance the load and effort moments, then divide.
silver.display: A wheelbarrow has its load of 150 N at 0.4 m from the wheel (pivot). The handles are 1.2 m from the wheel. Calculate the effort needed at the handles to lift the load.

guided_steps.say: Lever balance: load moment = effort moment. Load moment first.
Effort at 1.2 m must match: F × 1.2 = 60, so F = 60 ÷ 1.2. Clear the decimal by ×10: 600 ÷ 12.

guided_steps.hint: This should equal the load moment.

misconceptions.message: 60 Nm is the load's moment (150 × 0.4). Divide by the handle distance 1.2 m to get the effort: 50 N.
Balance: 150 × 0.4 = F × 1.2, so F = 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50 N. Swapping the distances (150 × 1.2 ÷ 0.4 = 450) uses the wrong arms.

problem_bank.gold_description: Multi-step: add several moments, include the beam's own weight, or chain a lever into a gear system.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, values already in the right units: use M = F × d or rearrange it.
problem_bank.silver_description: Convert a mass to weight first, or balance two moments and rearrange for the unknown.

worked_examples.question: A uniform beam is 2.0 m long and has a mass of 10 kg. The pivot is 0.8 m from the left end. A 50 N load hangs from the left end. Calculate the force needed at the right end to balance the beam. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
